Executive Director of Africa Education Watch, Kofi Asare, has called on the Ministry of Education to urgently intervene in the disagreement between the Rent Control Department and the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL) over hostel rents.
His comments follow an incident in which the Acting Rent Commissioner, Frederick Opoku, nearly got into a physical altercation with a hostel manager at the University of Ghana during the inspection at UGEL.
The confrontation reportedly followed a disagreement after Mr Opoku inspected the hostel facilities.
Speaking on Joy FM's Midday News on Wednesday, November 18, he said the Ministry should have been involved from the beginning, alongside Rent Control, the Parliamentary Select Committee on Education and university authorities.
This, he explained, is because the Select Committee approves rates, including the rent. He added that the stakeholders needed to examine UGEL's cost structure and profit margins to determine whether hostel rents could reasonably be reduced.
I think the Ministry of Education has a key role to play here. At the point of entry, Rent Control should have been working closely with the Ministry of Education, the Parliamentary Select Committee on Education, and the university authorities. And so all three bodies should have sat down and then went through the standardised build-up...Without that constructive engagement, it is impossible to make any progress in terms of reduction in rent,” he said.
Mr Asare said his organisation had advised about two months ago that the relevant stakeholders should engage to resolve the matter, but that had not happened.
He also criticised the approach adopted during recent Rent Control inspections, arguing that confrontations, verbal exchanges and public demonstrations would not address the underlying concerns.
“Waving around with cameras and bloggers and all that is not the solution to the problem we want to solve,” he said.
He added that hostel porters and managers were not responsible for determining rental rates, insisting that discussions should instead involve the institutions with the authority to influence the charges.
Mr Asare therefore urged the stakeholders to move beyond public exchanges and begin direct engagement on the cost of accommodation and possible rent reductions.
